SEAT Brand Could Be Phased Out as Cupra Prepares for Electric-Only Switchover
21 photos
Photo: Cupra
Even though Cupra wants to get rid of internal combustion at some point in the future, it simply does not know when. The problem with this outlook is that Cupra's best-selling model as of this writing is the Formentor, a compact-sized crossover that can be had with 1.5- to 2.5-liter mills. Indeed, the range-topping VZ5 specification uses the Audi turbocharged five-pot mill we all know and love.
At the same time, the SEAT brand is still trying to convince the Volkswagen Group that more affordable vehicles deserve another generation. Markus Haupt, who runs both of them, made his intentions clear at the Automobilwoche Congress in Berlin. As reported by Automotive News, the cooler marque with the pricier models is described by Haupt as the Spanish operation's growth engine.
The big kahuna also said that customer demand will dictate the switchover to electric-only models for Cupra , which is unbelievably vague. Adding insult to injury, the European Union has moved to replace its 2035 zero-emission mandate with a much softer fleet CO2 reduction target. Under the new arrangement, internal combustion and hybrid vehicles will remain on sale past 2035.
If you ask me, it's totally unsurprising how Cupra is now open to internal combustion vehicles for as long as there is demand for them. Automotive executives have spent years announcing electrification deadlines, only to discover that blindly following legislators doesn't automatically mean increased demand for electric vehicles in Spain and other European markets.
Cupra, meanwhile, depends heavily on combustion vehicles while its full-electric lineup matures. Cupra recorded nearly 224,000 registrations in Europe between January 2026 and September 2026, putting it well ahead of SEAT's 155,777-vehicle tally.
That's 44 percent in Cupra's favor, and the suits in Wolfsburg are right to get behind Cupra. They're not right in assuming that its growth means that SEAT may have to go.
Photo: Cupra It's been a few years since we first heard that SEAT may become an urban mobility brand or get discontinued altogether. The only certain thing we are currently aware of is that SEAT's current roadmap ends in 2029. Following the introduction of mild-hybrid variants for the Ibiza and Arona in 2027, the company outlined plans for a full-hybrid Leon in 2028. Come 2029, a bigger redesign may be on the menu.
Nothing has been publicly decided after 2029, though, and this is the reason why enthusiasts believe that Volkswagen is phasing out SEAT after its current products reach the end of their production life cycles. Martorell will remain busy regardless of what happens to said badge.
The Martorell plant has taken responsibility for production of the group's Electric Urban Car Family, which comprises four members: the Cupra Raval and Volkswagen ID. Polo hatchbacks on one hand, plus the Skoda Epiq and the Volkswagen ID. Cross front-drive crossovers on the other.
As opposed to a starting price of 16,900 euros in Spain for the internal combustion Polo, the zero-emission sibling is advertised at 17,900 euros from the outset, making it an interesting B-segment electric vehicle. The ID. Cross, meanwhile, slots between the T-Cross and Taigo in terms of pricing.
20,500 euros puts the ID. Cross higher than the Epiq, which is 18,500 euros for the most basic specification available in Spain. The Raval is the most expensive of the bunch in base flavor, with the Plus grade retailing at 28,610 euros in Spain.
